items.title: What do employers usually look at in hiring?

values: Materials and setup｜all fictional pendulum data

You are studying the relationship between pendulum length L and period T. The three sets of numbers below are purely teaching setups, not experimental measurements; use only paper or script calculations and do not build an apparatus.

A1: the reference gravitational acceleration is taken as 9.8 meters per second squared; the small-angle ideal model is T = 2 pi times the square root of L over g, ignoring air resistance and amplitude differences.
A2: the fictional data are L = 0.25, 0.36, and 0.49 meters, with measured T = 1.01, 1.20, and 1.42 seconds; the reading uncertainty for each T is provisionally set at plus or minus 0.03 seconds.
Tasks and deliverables
Calculate the three ideal periods, list and compare measured and model values, note meters, seconds, and residuals; plot T squared against L.
State which settings were not given: amplitude, number of timing runs, apparatus calibration; the residuals must not be interpreted as a proven new physical effect.
Reference approach (complete it yourself first)
The model periods are about 1.00, 1.20, and 1.40 seconds; the third residual is about +0.02 seconds, falling within the given plus or minus 0.03 second reading uncertainty.

T squared is approximately linear in L, but with only three fictional points the model cannot be proven to hold at any pendulum length and amplitude; before real measurement, a calibration and repetition plan should be proposed.
Boundaries and review
Review units, formulas, squaring, and rounding; keep the script and the original settings. The exercise requires no laser, high voltage, or any real experimental apparatus.

Read O*NET 19-2012 and the BLS education note and write the differences among theoretical, experimental, and computational tasks.

description.text: Physicist career guide: understand research questions, mathematical modeling, experiments and simulations, data validation, and education paths, and check United States 2025 wages and the 2025—2035 employment projection.

subject.name: Physicists
subject.summary: Physicists (United States SOC 19-2012) study the physical laws of matter, energy, space, and time. Common work is to pose testable questions, build mathematical models, design experiments or simulations, analyze data and uncertainty, review results, and publish or apply findings. Theory, experiment, and applied positions differ in tools and outputs. United States wages and projections correspond only to 19-2012; Chinese occupational wages, position qualifications, and research institution requirements require separate verification.
